claim: The hippocampus is critical for producing stable representations of familiar spaces.
source: The hippocampus is critical for producing stable representations of familiar spaces.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about hippocampal function.

claim: Changes to hippocampal inputs have not been measured during spatial learning.
source: How these representations arise is poorly understood, largely because changes to hippocampal inputs have not been measured during spatial learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gap in existing literature that the study addresses.

claim: Inputs driving place field spiking increased in amplitude during novel environment exploration.
source: Inputs driving place field spiking increased in amplitude – often suddenly – during novel environment exploration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the intracellular recordings presented in the study.

claim: Increases in input amplitude were not sustained in familiar environments.
source: However, these increases were not sustained in familiar environments.
evidence: This finding is based on comparisons between novel and familiar environment recordings.

claim: The spatial tuning of inputs became increasingly similar across repeated traversals of the environment with experience.
source: Rather, the spatial tuning of inputs became increasingly similar across repeated traversals of the environment with experience – both within fields and throughout the whole environment.
evidence: This is a key finding from spatial correlation analysis of subthreshold Vm.

claim: Complex spikes were not necessary for place field formation in novel environments.
source: In novel environments, CSs were not necessary for place field formation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on observations that place fields formed without CSs in novel environments.

claim: In humans, hippocampal damage results in an inability to convert ongoing experience into long-term memories.
source: In humans, hippocampal damage results in an inability to convert the ongoing experience of items and events from daily life into long-term memories (Scoville and Milner, 1957).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to classic work by Scoville and Milner.

claim: In rodents, the hippocampus is critically involved in encoding spatial layouts and locations of importance.
source: In rodents, the hippocampus has been shown to be critically involved in encoding spatial layouts and locations of importance (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Morris et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational rodent hippocampus studies.

claim: Neural representations of novel environments form rapidly in the rodent hippocampus.
source: Neural representations of novel (i.e., previously unencountered) environments form rapidly in the rodent hippocampus (Hill, 1978; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Frank et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Place field activity stabilizes with experience.
source: Place field activity stabilizes (i.e., becomes more similar across successive traversals of the environment) with experience (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Frank et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004; Cacucci et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous extracellular recording studies.

claim: The persistence of place fields over time provides the neural basis of spatial memory.
source: the persistence of fields over time provides the neural basis of spatial memory (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Thompson and Best, 1990; Liu et al., 2012; Mankin et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations linking place field persistence to memory.

claim: Synaptic plasticity has been strongly implicated in spatial learning-based behaviors.
source: Synaptic plasticity has been strongly implicated in spatial learning-based behaviors (Morris, 1989; Tsien et al., 1996) as well as changes in place field activity (Bostock et al., 1991; McHugh et al., 1996; Mehta et al., 1997, 2000, 2002; Ekstrom et al., 2001; Lever et al., 2002; Cacucci et al., 2007; Bittner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to plasticity studies.

claim: Pharmacological and genetic manipulations of NMDA receptors suggest that synaptic plasticity is not needed for place fields to appear in novel environments.
source: Pharmacological and genetic manipulations of NMDA receptors (NMDARs) suggest that synaptic plasticity is not needed for place fields to appear in novel environments (McHugh et al., 1996; Kentros et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to NMDAR manipulation studies.

claim: Intracellular recordings suggest that specific, plasticity-inducing events are required to generate each new place field.
source: However, intracellular recordings suggest that specific, plasticity-inducing events are required to generate each new place field (Bittner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific intracellular recording study.

claim: Complex-spike events trigger synaptic plasticity in vitro.
source: intracellular experiments have shown that large, calcium-mediated complex-spike (CS) events (Kandel and Spencer, 1961; Wong and Prince, 1978; Traub and Llinás, 1979; Harvey et al., 2009; Epsztein et al., 2011; Grienberger et al., 2014), which trigger synaptic plasticity in vitro (Takahashi and Magee, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to in vitro plasticity studies.

claim: Complex spikes are sufficient to artificially create place fields.
source: which trigger synaptic plasticity in vitro (Takahashi and Magee, 2009) and are sufficient to artificially create place fields
evidence: This claim is based on previous experimental work cited in the introduction.

claim: Complex spikes always co-occur with the spontaneous appearance of new fields in familiar environments.
source: and are sufficient to artificially create place fields, always co-occur with the spontaneous appearance of new fields in familiar environments (Bittner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bittner et al., 2015.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 place field firing rates increase with repeated traversals through each location within a behavioral session.
source: Within a behavioral session, hippocampal CA1 place field firing rates increase with repeated traversals through each location (Mehta et al., 1997, 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The average firing rate of CA1 place cells is lower in familiar compared to novel environments across days.
source: Across days, though, the opposite occurs, with the average firing rate of CA1 place cells being lower in familiar compared to novel environments (Nitz and McNaughton, 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reliability of where a place cell fires increases with experience.
source: However, when a place cell fires, the reliability of where it fires increases with experience (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Leutgeb et al., 2004; Cacucci et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whole-cell intracellular recordings of hippocampal neurons were obtained in mice exploring both novel and familiar environments.
source: Therefore, we performed whole-cell intracellular recordings of hippocampal neurons in mice exploring both novel and familiar environments
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Intracellular recording allows access to inputs via the subthreshold membrane potential.
source: Unlike extracellular recording, intracellular recording allows access to inputs via the subthreshold membrane potential (Vm), to CSs, and to intrinsic cellular properties such as the AP threshold that shape how inputs are converted into spiking output.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical capabilities of intracellular recording.

claim: Virtual reality-based methods were employed in which animals moved through visually defined virtual environments by running in place.
source: Our experiments employed virtual reality-based methods in which animals moved through visually defined virtual environments by running in place (Hölscher et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2013; Ravassard et al., 2013)
evidence: This describes the experimental methods with supporting citations.

claim: The peak amplitude of the main subthreshold Vm hill increased between the initial and late laps in novel environments.
source: In novel environments, the peak amplitude increased between the initial (1–2) and late (6-end) laps (Figure 3A, left, 3B)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The peak subthreshold Vm in novel mazes increased from 1.9 ± 0.5 mV in initial laps to 3.1 ± 0.6 mV in late laps (p=0.003, n=14).
source: This was the case when considering the peak subthreshold Vm within the field determined from the average subthreshold Vm as a function of location over the entire epoch (median ± SE, NOV initial laps: 1.9 ± 0.5 mV, late laps: 3.1 ± 0.6, p=0.003, n = 14, Figure 3A, left)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: No increases in subthreshold Vm amplitude were observed within familiar mazes.
source: In contrast, no increases in amplitude were observed within familiar mazes (p=0.47, Figure 3A, right; lap peak: p=0.70).
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The increase in amplitude is consistent with a strengthening of inputs to place fields via Hebbian, spike timing-dependent, or other mechanisms of synaptic plasticity.
source: The increase in amplitude is consistent with a strengthening of inputs to place fields via Hebbian, spike timing-dependent, or other (Golding et al., 2002; Dudman et al., 2007) mechanisms of synaptic plasticity
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with supporting citations.

claim: The peak subthreshold Vm in the place field increased sharply from the laps before to the laps after spiking began in novel epochs where place field spiking did not occur in the first lap.
source: For the subset of novel epochs in which place field spiking did not occur in the first lap, the peak subthreshold Vm in the place field increased sharply from the laps before to the laps after spiking began (Figure 3C–D and E, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: There was no consistent increase in peak subthreshold Vm after the first spiking lap.
source: However, there was no consistent increase after the first spiking lap, including cases in which place field spiking occurred in the first lap of the epoch (First-Active lap: 4.0 ± 0.9 mV, Post' laps: 4.1 ± 0.5, n = 9, p=1.0, Figure 3E, right).
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The sharp increase in subthreshold Vm suggests mechanisms of plasticity that do not rely on postsynaptic spiking.
source: The sharp increase suggests mechanisms of plasticity that do not rely on postsynaptic spiking (Golding et al., 2002; Dudman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with supporting citations.

claim: In all five cases where place field spiking was not present in the first lap of a novel epoch, the mean Vm in the laps before spiking was greater inside versus outside the eventual place field.
source: In all five cases in which place field spiking was not present in the first lap of a novel epoch, the mean Vm in the laps before spiking was greater inside versus outside the eventual place field (Figure 3F; also see Figure 3C–D, bottom right).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Inputs were biased towards the locations of the place fields before spiking occurred.
source: This suggests that inputs were biased towards the locations of the place fields before spiking occurred.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Vm was higher in eventual place field locations before spiking.

claim: The peak firing rate of active cells was higher in novel environments (5.9 ± 2.1 Hz) than familiar environments (1.7 ± 0.5 Hz) (p=0.004, n=10).
source: First, in agreement with previous extracellular recordings from freely moving rats (Nitz and McNaughton, 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008), the peak firing rate of active cells was higher in novel environments (peak of average firing rate as a function of location over the entire epoch, NOV: 5.9 ± 2.1 Hz, FAM: 1.7 ± 0.5, n = 10 NOV-FAM maze pairs with at least one epoch being active, p=0.004, Figure 3G
evidence: This finding is supported by data and agrees with previous studies.

claim: The proportion of cells that were active was greater in novel (69%) than familiar (47%) environments.
source: and the proportion of cells that were active was greater (69% of NOV epochs and 47% of FAM epochs).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: The spike threshold did not differ between novel and familiar environments.
source: However, we found that the spike threshold (Figure 4A) and baseline (Figure 4B) did not differ between novel and familiar environments.
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The baseline Vm did not differ between novel and familiar environments.
source: However, we found that the spike threshold (Figure 4A) and baseline (Figure 4B) did not differ between novel and familiar environments.
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The amplitude of the peak subthreshold Vm was smaller in familiar environments (1.8 ± 0.2 mV) than novel environments (2.4 ± 0.4 mV) (p=0.042, n=14).
source: Instead, the amplitude of the peak subthreshold Vm was smaller in familiar environments (NOV: 2.4 ± 0.4 mV, FAM: 1.8 ± 0.2, n = 14 active and silent NOV-FAM maze pairs, p=0.042, Figure 3H
evidence: This is a key quantitative finding from the data.

claim: There was no sign that any part of the increase in amplitude during novel exploration remained by the time environments became familiar.
source: Furthermore, there was no sign that any part of the increase in amplitude during novel exploration remained by the time environments became familiar (p=0.52, Figure 3J, left).
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The second highest subthreshold Vm peak in each environment was not larger in novel compared to familiar environments.
source: The second highest subthreshold Vm peak in each environment was not, however, larger in novel compared to familiar environments (NOV: 1.4 ± 0.1 mV, FAM: 1.4 ± 0.1, n = 14, p=1.0).
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: Somatic input resistance did not differ between novel and familiar mazes.
source: However, somatic RN did not differ between novel and familiar mazes (p=0.30, Figure 4C)
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The number of spikes evoked by depolarizing current steps did not differ between novel and familiar environments.
source: However, the number of spikes evoked by depolarizing current steps (0.1–0.2 nA, 0.1 s) did not differ between novel and familiar environments (p=0.55, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The AP threshold was negatively correlated with the mean AP rate in novel mazes.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Epsztein et al., 2011), we found that the AP threshold was negatively correlated with the mean AP rate in novel mazes (p=0.041, Figure 4E, top).
evidence: This finding is supported by data and agrees with previous work.

claim: No correlation was found between AP threshold and mean AP rate in familiar mazes.
source: Interestingly, no such correlation was found in familiar mazes
evidence: This is a negative result from correlation analysis.

claim: In familiar mazes, the mean AP rate was positively correlated with the baseline Vm.
source: for which the mean AP rate was instead positively correlated with the baseline Vm (p=0.003, Figure 4F, bottom right).
evidence: This is a positive result from correlation analysis.

claim: The baseline Vm was more depolarized in epochs with ≥1 AP than in epochs with no spontaneous activity for both novel and familiar mazes.
source: In addition, the baseline Vm was more depolarized in epochs with ≥1 AP than in epochs with no spontaneous activity for both novel and familiar mazes (NOV: p=0.002, FAM: p<0.001, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a positive result from statistical comparison.

claim: In a novel environment, intrinsic cellular excitability helps to determine the initial place field representation.
source: These results suggest that in a novel environment, intrinsic cellular excitability helps to determine the initial place field representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between AP threshold and firing rate in novel environments.

claim: When the environment has become familiar, inputs can drive the stored spatial representations in CA1 irrespective of excitability.
source: Then, when the environment has become familiar, inputs can drive the stored spatial representations in CA1 irrespective of excitability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of correlation between AP threshold and firing rate in familiar environments.

claim: Subthreshold Vm spatial correlation scores were significantly lower in novel (0.58 ± 0.12) than familiar (0.69 ± 0.03) mazes (p=0.003).
source: In contrast, the subthreshold Vm spatial correlation scores were significantly lower in novel than familiar mazes (NOV: 0.58 ± 0.12, FAM: 0.69 ± 0.03, p=0.003, Figure 5B, middle left).
evidence: This is a key quantitative finding from spatial correlation analysis.

claim: The Vm correlation scores were lower in the initial laps of novel environments and significantly increased across laps within a novel but not familiar epoch.
source: Moreover, the Vm correlation scores were lower in the initial laps (p=0.003, Figure 5B, middle right), then significantly increased across laps within a novel but not familiar epoch, reaching close to the familiar values in later laps (Figure 5B, middle right).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The progressive stabilization of spatial tuning with experience is an intracellular signature of the establishment of a long-term memory trace.
source: This progressive stabilization of spatial tuning with experience is an intracellular signature of the establishment of a long-term memory trace.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial correlation findings.

claim: The out-field subthreshold Vm correlation scores started low in the initial laps of novel environments then increased in the later laps, and in familiar mazes were generally well-correlated across laps.
source: As with the overall spatial correlation scores, the out-field scores started low in the initial laps (p=0.008) of novel environments then increased in the later laps, and in familiar mazes were generally well-correlated across laps (Figure 5B, bottom).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For the subset of epochs in which cells were silent, the spatial correlation of the subthreshold Vm also increased during novel exploration and was high in familiar environments.
source: Furthermore, for the subset of epochs in which cells were silent, the spatial correlation of the subthreshold Vm also increased during novel exploration and was high in familiar environments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The increase in spatial tuning was not limited to the place field region, and the spatial tuning of the rest of the inputs also stabilizes.
source: These results indicate that the increase in spatial tuning was not limited to the place field region, and that the spatial tuning of the rest of the inputs also stabilizes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the out-field and silent cell correlation findings.

claim: The lower Vm correlation scores in novel mazes were not attributable to differences in running behavior.
source: However, the lower Vm correlation scores in novel mazes were not attributable to differences in running behavior, as speed correlation scores did not predict Vm correlation scores (p=0.28; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a negative result from correlation analysis.

claim: Signs of a backward shift of the subthreshold Vm hill with experience and a negative skew were observed.
source: A backward shift of the hill with experience (i.e., a shift in location in the direction opposite to the animal's motion) (Blum and Abbott, 1996; Mehta et al., 1997) and a negative skew (i.e., a slower rise in the direction of the animal's motion) (Mehta et al., 2000; 2002; Ekstrom et al., 2001; Harvey et al., 2009) are thought to result from spike timing-dependent plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998). Signs of both were observed in the subthreshold Vm hills underlying the AP place field (Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This finding is supported by data and previous theoretical work.

claim: Complex spikes occurred in novel and familiar mazes and had similar properties in both.
source: CSs occurred in novel and familiar mazes and had similar properties in both (e.g., duration, number of APs, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Complex spikes spontaneously occurred at low rates in both novel (14 CSs total in 10 of 190 total laps) and familiar (17 CSs in 11/228 laps) mazes.
source: CSs spontaneously occurred at low rates in both novel (14 CSs total in 10 of 190 total laps from nine maze epochs with ≥1 AP) and familiar (17 CSs in 11/228 laps from 26 epochs) mazes
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: Of the nine novel epoch place fields, four displayed stable activity in the place field region prior to any CSs.
source: Of the nine novel epoch place fields, four displayed stable activity in the place field region prior to any CSs (which then occurred later in the place field in 3/4 cases, e.g., Figure 6A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: Two novel epoch place fields had ≥1 CS in the initial lap of the emergent field.
source: two had ≥1 CS in the initial lap of the emergent field (e.g., Figures 3C and 6B)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: Three novel epoch place fields were in epochs that did not have any CSs.
source: and the remaining 3 were in epochs that did not have any CSs (e.g., Figures 2B and 3D did not contain CSs).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: CSs were not required for place field formation in novel environments.
source: Thus, CSs were not required for place field formation in novel environments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that place fields formed without CSs.

claim: CSs in familiar mazes did not necessarily stabilize place fields.
source: Moreover, CSs in familiar mazes did not necessarily stabilize place fields (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A transient, but significant, increase in AP rate was found in the first lap after the first CS.
source: We found a transient, but significant, increase in AP rate in the first lap after the first CS (Figure 6C, top)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No transient increase was found in subsequent peak subthreshold Vm activity after the first CS.
source: but not in subsequent peak subthreshold Vm activity (Figure 6C, bottom).
evidence: This is a negative result from the data analysis.

claim: A transient increase in AP rate and subthreshold Vm spatial correlation scores was found after the first CS.
source: Regarding spatial tuning, we found a transient increase in AP rate and subthreshold Vm spatial correlation scores after the first CS
evidence: This finding is from the spatial correlation analysis.

claim: Individual CSs appear to contribute an amount to plasticity and spatial learning that varies in magnitude.
source: Therefore, individual CSs appear to contribute an amount to plasticity and spatial learning that varies in magnitude – from small (i.e., transient increases in spiking and spatial correlation) to potentially large (i.e., occurring in the first lap of new place fields).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the variable effects of CSs observed in the data.

claim: Initial inhomogeneities in inputs are amplified to produce robust place field activity without the need for plasticity.
source: initially, small inhomogeneities in spatial inputs and excitability present during the first experience in an environment are amplified to produce robust place field activity without the need for plasticity
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Plasticity during repeated traversals of the environment progressively refines and stabilizes the representation for long-term storage.
source: plasticity during repeated traversals of the environment progressively refines and stabilizes this representation for long-term storage
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: After learning, the inputs are no longer amplified, but the stability of these less strongly modulated inputs yields reliable spatially tuned firing.
source: after learning, the inputs are no longer amplified, but the stability of these less strongly modulated inputs yields reliable spatially tuned firing.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: The role of plasticity is to capture the initial representation and stabilize it before the network changes again.
source: That is, the role of plasticity is to capture the initial representation and stabilize it before the network changes again, perhaps as a result of learning in other contexts in intervening periods.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the role of plasticity based on the findings.

claim: The initial expansion of activity could provide a diversity of synaptic and cellular patterns from which a sparser representation of space can be selected for long-term stabilization.
source: The initial expansion of activity (i.e., greater numbers of more active cells) could provide a diversity of synaptic and cellular patterns from which a sparser representation of space can be selected for long-term stabilization.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The amplification of spiking activity could serve to drive plasticity in downstream targets or send a general novelty signal to the rest of the brain.
source: The amplification of spiking activity could also serve to drive plasticity in downstream targets (Lisman, 1997; Harris et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2012) or send a general novelty signal (Duncan et al., 2012; Larkin et al., 2014) to the rest of the brain
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: The comparatively low amplitude of inputs and firing rate in familiar environments may function to limit changes to the representation, further contributing to its stability.
source: Afterwards, the comparatively low amplitude of inputs and firing rate in familiar environments may function to limit changes to the representation, further contributing to its stability.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Variability of the low amplitude, but spatially reliable, modulation of inputs across the environment could explain why a given place cell is not always active in the same environment, but that when it fires, it does so in the same location.
source: Variability of the low amplitude, but spatially reliable, modulation of inputs across the environment could explain why a given place cell is not always active in the same environment, but that when it fires, it does so in the same location (Ziv et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: There is no difference in the average firing rates of excitatory neurons in CA3 or EC in novel compared to familiar environments.
source: To begin with, there could be increased activity in input areas. However, the evidence to date indicates no difference in the average firing rates of excitatory neurons in CA3 (Karlsson and Frank, 2008) or EC (Barry et al., 2012) in novel compared to familiar environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neuromodulators such as acetylcholine and dopamine could underlie a novelty-specific enhancement of inputs.
source: Neuromodulators such as acetylcholine (Hasselmo, 2006; Teles-Grilo Ruivo and Mellor, 2013) and dopamine (Li et al., 2003; Kentros et al., 2004; McNamara et al., 2014; Takeuchi et al., 2016) could underlie a novelty-specific enhancement of inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: The correlation between spike rate and AP threshold in novel but not familiar environments is consistent with a model in which initial differences in intrinsic excitability bias which cells will be originally recruited into a given memory representation.
source: The correlation between spike rate and AP threshold in novel but not familiar environments (Figure 4E) is consistent with a model in which initial differences in intrinsic excitability bias which cells will be originally recruited into a given memory representation, with changes in excitability over time resulting in the allocation of different sets of cells to subsequent experiences (Han et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2009; Epsztein et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2016; Rashid et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with supporting citations.

claim: The lack of correlation between firing rate and threshold in familiar environments suggests that, after the stabilization of a representation, inputs determine activity irrespective of excitability levels.
source: In particular, the lack of correlation between firing rate and threshold in familiar environments suggests that, after the stabilization of a representation, inputs determine activity irrespective of excitability levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: The correlation between firing rate and baseline Vm in familiar environments suggests that learning leads to the emergence of a cell assembly representing each maze.
source: Furthermore, the correlation between firing rate and baseline Vm in familiar environments (Figure 4F) suggests that learning leads to the emergence of a cell assembly (Hebb, 1949) representing each maze, resulting in a spatially uniform subthreshold depolarizing bias for all place cells active in a given environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with supporting citation.

claim: The inputs driving place fields may have remained strengthened in familiar mazes, but the out-of-field inputs may also have strengthened with familiarization, thus reducing the amplitude of the hill relative to the baseline.
source: In this case, the lower amplitude of the Vm hills under place fields in familiar mazes may not represent weaker inputs. Rather, the inputs driving place fields may have remained strengthened, but the out-of-field inputs may also have strengthened with familiarization, thus reducing the amplitude of the hill relative to the baseline.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The higher firing rate of inhibitory neurons in CA1 in familiar environments could reduce the Vm everywhere, keeping the average cell's baseline Vm similar to that in novel environments.
source: Meanwhile, the higher firing rate of inhibitory neurons in CA1 in familiar environments (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Frank et al., 2004; Nitz and McNaughton, 2004) could reduce the Vm everywhere, keeping the average cell's baseline Vm similar to that in novel environments, thereby masking the presence of these strengthened synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Thirty-two cells were recorded from 15 mice navigating in virtual mazes.
source: Thirty-two cells were recorded from 15 mice navigating in virtual mazes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample size.

claim: Cells were active in 47% of epochs in familiar mazes and 69% of epochs in novel mazes.
source: Cells were active (where 'active' was defined as follows: peak AP firing rate as a function of location averaged over the maze epoch ≥0.5 Hz and spiking in ≥2 laps) in 47% of epochs in familiar mazes (21/45 epochs, 15/29 cells) and 69% of epochs in novel mazes (9/13 epochs, 8/12 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: The animals' licking shifted from occurring just after reward delivery at the primary reward zone in novel environments to occurring just before delivery in familiar environments.
source: The animals' licking shifted from occurring just after reward delivery at the primary reward zone in novel environments to occurring just before delivery (i.e., predictively) in familiar environments (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), providing behavioral evidence of spatial learning.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and provides behavioral evidence of learning.

claim: Each cell's location-based activity with respect to a common reference was uncorrelated across distinct mazes, suggestive of global remapping between the virtual environments.
source: Each cell's location-based activity with respect to a common reference (the fixed-location primary reward zone) was uncorrelated across distinct mazes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggestive of global remapping (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Muller and Kubie, 1987; Leutgeb et al., 2005) between the virtual environments.
evidence: This finding is supported by data and suggests global remapping with supporting citations.

claim: Animals ran at similar overall speeds in novel (16.6 ± 1.3 cm/s) and familiar (15.8 ± 0.7 cm/s) mazes (p=0.63).
source: Animals ran at similar overall speeds (NOV: 16.6 ± 1.3 cm/s, FAM: 15.8 ± 0.7, n = 14, p=0.63, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is a negative result from statistical comparison.

claim: The instantaneous speed of the animal was not correlated with the instantaneous subthreshold Vm across novel and familiar epochs.
source: Furthermore, the instantaneous speed of the animal was not correlated with the instantaneous subthreshold Vm across novel and familiar epochs (median ± SE of Pearson's r value per epoch: 0.01 ± 0.02, p=1.0).
evidence: This is a negative result from correlation analysis.

claim: Theta-band power was slightly positively correlated with mean subthreshold Vm.
source: As in freely moving rats (Lee et al., 2012), the theta-band power was slightly positively correlated with mean subthreshold Vm (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This finding is supported by data and agrees with previous work.

claim: Slightly increased in-field theta power (5–10 Hz power1/2 in mV, NOV: 0.79 ± 0.09, FAM: 0.68 ± 0.06, p<0.001) was found in novel mazes.
source: Indeed, we found slightly increased in-field theta power (5–10 Hz power1/2 in mV, NOV: 0.79 ± 0.09, FAM: 0.68 ± 0.06, n = 14, p<0.001)
